title: Urban soundscape categorization based on individual recognition, perception, and assessment of sound environments
research_question: How are groups classified according to sound source identification? Are there differences in soundscape perceptions for each attention cluster? Are perceptual components derived from typical (ISO 12913-2) and extensive attributes (Swedish rating scale)? How is the relationship between soundscape indicators (acoustic parameters and sound source identification) and descriptors (perceived affective and overall quality) different for each cluster?

participants.description: 25 male, 25 female; 20-41 years (mean age: 23.82, SD: 3.06). Undergraduate and graduate students from the same university, familiar with the 10 sites in Seoul's Gangbuk area, with normal hearing.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 10 urban environments in Seoul's Gangbuk area (2 green spaces, 2 public spaces, 2 urban streets, 2 open squares, 2 open spaces). Audio-visual stimuli recorded with a six-channel 360 spherical camera (Insta 360 pro, 8k UHD, 30 fps, 95 Mbps) and a four-channel ambisonic microphone (Soundfield SPS 200, FOA ambisonic setup). Sound pressure levels calibrated. Presented via head-mounted display (VIVE Pro, HTC) and open-type headphones (HD-650, Sennheiser). Each stimulus was 3 minutes long.

measures.instrument: Likert scale (1=not at all to 5=dominates the space) for traffic noise, human sounds, natural sounds, and other noises.
8 typical unidirectional attributes (pleasant, chaotic, vibrant, uneventful, calm, annoying, eventful, monotonous) on a 5-point Likert scale (1=strongly disagree to 5=strongly agree).
116 extensive unidirectional attributes (Swedish rating scale) on a 100-mm visual analog scale (0=no match to 100=perfect match).
"Overall, how would you describe the surrounding sound environment?" (1=very bad to 5=very good).
"Overall, to what extent is the surrounding sound environment appropriate for the location?" (1=not at all to 5=perfectly).
LAeq (A-weighted sound pressure level), LA10-A90 (temporal variations), LCeq-Aeq (low-frequency characteristics), Loudness (sone), Sharpness (acum).

findings.mechanism: Participants were clustered into three groups based on their sound source identification patterns: Cluster 1 (attentive to traffic noise and other noises), Cluster 2 (less attentive to the sound environment), and Cluster 3 (attentive to natural and human sounds).
findings.source: 3.1.2. Clustering based on sound source identification, p.5
findings.quote: Their categorizations by sound source identification were divided into three clusters
Traffic noise showed a weak positive relationship with LCeq-Aeq (r = 0.15, p < 0.05)

findings.mechanism: Human sounds are an important cognitive factor exhibiting relatively high frequency characteristics.
findings.quote: human sounds had a strong positive relationship with LAeq (r = 0.57, p < 0.01)
loudness (r = 0.52, p < 0.05)

findings.mechanism: Human sounds exhibit relatively high frequency characteristics, recognized differently from general low frequencies.
findings.quote: a negative relationship with LCeq-Aeq (r = -0.49, p < 0.01)

findings.mechanism: Natural sounds are a determining factor of temporal variations in sound environments.
findings.quote: For natural sounds, LA10-A90 (r = 0.32, p < 0.01) showed the highest positive relationship

findings.mechanism: Other noise (ventilation and air conditioning systems) are a determining factor of low frequency characteristics.
findings.quote: Other noise had a positive relationship with LCeq-Aeq (r = 0.32, p < 0.01)

findings.quote: post-hoc comparison results (Scheffé method) found a significant difference between Clusters 2 and 3 in positive expressions of space (p < 0.05)

findings.mechanism: PCA revealed that for the entire group, Cluster 1, and Cluster 3, typical attributes loaded onto Supportive (positive attributes) and Detrimental (negative attributes) components.
findings.quote: The entire group (All), Cluster 1, and Cluster 3 were classified by Component 1, involving positive attributes (vibrant, eventful, and pleasant) and supportive soundscapes, and Component 2, comprising negative attributes (annoying and chaotic) and detrimental soundscapes

findings.mechanism: PCA revealed that for Cluster 2, typical attributes loaded onto a unique Tranquil component (calm, uneventful, monotonous).
findings.quote: Cluster 2 revealed a different important perceptual component: tranquil soundscapes (Component 3), constituting calm, uneventful, and monotonous attributes. Its explanatory power was 29%

findings.mechanism: PCA revealed that for the entire group, Cluster 1, and Cluster 3, extensive attributes loaded onto Supportive, Detrimental, and Tranquil components.
findings.quote: The entire group (All), Cluster 1 and Cluster 3 combined three perceptual components: (1) supportive soundscapes, involving positive attributes (appealing, interesting, exciting, attractive, and lively) (explanatory power: 22–26%), (2) detrimental soundscapes, represent-ing negative attributes (dreary, irritable, ugly, and undesirable) (explanatory power: 16–19%), and (3) tranquil soundscapes, comprising calm, tranquil, quiet, and static attributes (explanatory power: 10–12%).

findings.consequent: Perceptual components (Supportive, Detrimental, Relaxed, Tranquil) for Cluster 2
findings.mechanism: PCA revealed that for Cluster 2, extensive attributes loaded onto Supportive, Detrimental, Relaxed, and Tranquil components, with different explanatory power levels.
findings.quote: Cluster 2 categorized a fourth perceptual component, relaxed soundscapes, comprising cozy, comfortable, and naturally relaxed soundscapes, and revealed different explanatory power levels for each component. Detrimental soundscape was the highest (18%), while supportive soundscape was the lowest (10%).
